title: First-Time Car Buyer Checklist: What to Bring to the Dealership
summary: Bring a valid driver's license, proof of insurance, proof of income, proof of address and your trade-in paperwork if you have one. Having these ready, plus a budget you've already worked out, turns your first car purchase into a quick, low-stress visit.
key_takeaways: Bring your driver's license, proof of insurance, recent pay stubs and a recent bill with your address.
If you're trading in a car, bring its title or loan payoff details and all keys.
Decide on a monthly budget before you shop, not at the desk.
A pre-approval from your bank or credit union gives you a number to compare against.
Ask questions. A good dealership is happy to slow down and explain.

sections.heading: What documents do I need to buy my first car?
paragraphs: Most first-time buyers need four things: a valid driver's license, proof of car insurance, proof of income and proof of address. With those in hand, most purchases can be finished in one visit.

Proof of income is usually your two or three most recent pay stubs. If you're self-employed, recent bank statements or tax returns often work instead. Proof of address can be a recent utility bill, bank statement or lease agreement with your name on it.
Exact requirements can vary by lender and by state, so it's always fine to call ahead and ask what to bring.

sections.heading: What should I bring if I'm trading in a car?
paragraphs: Bring the car's title if you own it outright. If you still owe money on it, bring your lender's name and your account number so the payoff can be confirmed.
Also bring the registration, every key and remote you have, and any service records. Spare keys and a clean maintenance history can help your trade-in value.

sections.heading: How do I set a budget before I shop?
paragraphs: Start with what you can comfortably pay each month, then add insurance, fuel and basic maintenance. Many people find it helpful to keep their total car costs well under a fifth of their take-home pay, but the right number depends on your other bills and goals.
Write your number down and bring it with you. It keeps the conversation focused on cars that genuinely fit your life.

sections.heading: Should I get pre-approved for a loan first?
paragraphs: A pre-approval isn't required, but it's a smart move. A bank or credit union pre-approval tells you roughly how much you can borrow and at what rate, so you have something to compare against.
Dealerships often work with several lenders and may be able to find you a competitive option too. Having a pre-approval simply means you can compare offers with confidence.

sections.heading: What should I check before I sign?
paragraphs: Take a real test drive on roads you normally use, including the highway if you commute. Check that everything works: lights, air conditioning, heat, windows, and the infotainment screen.

For a used car, ask for a vehicle history report. Before you sign, read the final numbers: the vehicle price, any add-ons, taxes and fees, the loan length and the monthly payment. If anything is unclear, ask. It's your money, and good salespeople expect questions.

sections.heading: Where can I get help with my first purchase?
paragraphs: If you're shopping in the area, Your Dealership Name is happy to walk first-time buyers through every step, from paperwork to picking the right car. Give us a call before you come in and we'll tell you exactly what to bring.

faq.question: Can I buy a car without a credit history?
faq.answer: Often, yes. Some lenders offer first-time buyer programs, and a larger down payment or a co-signer can help. Options depend on your income and the lender, so ask what's available for your situation.

faq.question: Do I need insurance before I drive the car home?
faq.answer: In most states, yes. You'll usually need to show proof of insurance for the new car before you can drive it off the lot. Call your insurance company ahead of time so the switch is quick.

faq.question: How long does it take to buy a car at a dealership?
faq.answer: If you bring the right documents and know your budget, many purchases take a few hours or less. Financing approval and trade-in appraisal are usually the longest steps.

faq.question: Is it okay to bring someone with me?
faq.answer: Absolutely. A trusted friend or family member can help you notice things during the test drive and remember questions you want to ask.
